title: Declarative Client Adapter Blueprint
content:
Purpose
---
Personal sketch: capture a compact, declarative config model and minimal runtime contract for a Client Adapter that sits in front of Redwood API calls inside customer apps and SDKs. Goal: make routing, retries, cost-aware fallbacks, and telemetry wiring configurable without bespoke application logic. This is a working brain-dump for design review.

High-level goals / constraints
- Very small surface area for app developers: one adapter config object + SDK init hook.
- Deterministic semantics: config is declarative and evaluated in a deterministic order (no hidden side-effects).
- Composable policies: routing, fallback, and batching as composable primitives.
- Instrumentation-first: every decision emits stable telemetry keys for offline analysis.
- Backwards-compat: fallback to current call shapes used by hosted API; adapter should act as a thin shim.
- Lightweight: keep client-side logic tiny: mostly policy evaluation + minimal network calls to a local control plane.

Core concepts (v0)
- Adapter config (declarative): YAML/JSON blob embedded in app or served from CDN/Config service.
- Route: mapping of a logical request (labels) -> candidate model endpoints and policies.
- Policy types: routing (priority/cost), fallback (sequence of fallbacks), throttle (rate caps), batchHint (soft batching suggestions), telemetry (sample rates + key tags).
- Condition expressions: small boolean DSL referencing request labels, e.g., user_tier == "enterprise" and latency_sensitive == true.
- Telemetry emission: decision events (ROUTE_CHOSEN, FALLBACK_TRIGGERED, BATCH_SENT), attach route_id and policy_ids.

Example adapter config (YAML)
- Note: this is intentionally minimal and plain to be copy-paste friendly in SDKs.

config_version: 1
routes:
  - id: quick-reply
    match: request.intent == "reply_short" or request.max_tokens <= 24
    routing:
      - candidate: hosted:base-gptq-3b
        priority: 10
        perf_hint: low-latency
      - candidate: dedicated:sm-quant-3b
        priority: 20
        perf_hint: balanced
    fallback_policy:
      mode: sequential
      steps:
        - on_error: rate_limit
          fallback_to: hosted:base-gptq-3b-lowcost
        - on_error: latency_exceeded
          fallback_to: hosted:fast-2.7b
    telemetry:
      sample_rate: 0.05
      tags: ["feature:in-app-compose"]

  - id: heavy-embed
    match: request.type == "embed" and request.corpus_size > 10000
    routing:
      - candidate: dedicated:embed-32k
        priority: 5
        perf_hint: throughput
    throttle:
      qps: 2
      burst: 5
    telemetry:
      sample_rate: 0.2

Runtime contract (SDK-adapter interaction)
- Init: SDK calls Adapter.init({config, onTelemetry}) where config is the blob above and onTelemetry is a callback to forward events.
- Evaluate: For each request, SDK wraps request with labels and calls Adapter.route(req). Adapter returns an ordered list of candidate endpoints plus metadata (route_id, reason_tags, telemetry_context).
- Submit: SDK uses the top candidate to issue a normal Redwood API call; adapter can optionally provide an alternative tokenization hint or max_tokens override where supported.
- Fallback loop: SDK monitors response; on error or SLA miss it calls Adapter.onOutcome(outcome) which returns next candidate or a terminal verdict.

Adapter API shape (JS-ish pseudotype)
- init(config: string|object, opts?: {onTelemetry?: (evt) => void}) -> Promise<void>
- route(req: {labels: Record<string,any>, payloadPreview?: string}) -> Promise<{candidates: string[], route_id: string, meta: string[]}>
- onOutcome(outcome: {route_id: string, candidate: string, status: "ok"|"error"|"latency_miss", error_code?: string, metrics?: {latency_ms?: number, tokens?: number}}) -> Promise<{next: string|null, terminal_reason?: string}>

Notes about labels and payloadPreview
- labels are the primary signal for route matching; they should be small key-values set by app logic (user_tier, latency_sensitive, request.type, intent, expected_tokens, cost_constraint).
- payloadPreview is an optional short string (<=512 bytes) used by local heuristics to decide batch grouping and perf hints but NOT sent to Redwood control plane. Privacy: avoid PII.

Telemetry & observability
- Mandatory events emitted via onTelemetry: ROUTE_EVALUATED, CANDIDATE_SELECTED, FALLBACK_ATTEMPT, OUTCOME_RECORDED, CONFIG_REFRESH.
- Each event must include stable fields: timestamp_iso, route_id, client_id_hash, policy_ids[], decision_reason[], sample_rate, config_version.
- Design note: include a compact route fingerprint (route_id) and human-readable label for offline analysis.

Sequence diagram (ASCII)
App -> SDK: send request
SDK -> Adapter: route(req)
Adapter -> SDK: {candidate: hosted:fast-2.7b, route_id: quick-reply}
SDK -> Redwood API: gen request to hosted:fast-2.7b
Redwood -> SDK: response (slow) or error
SDK -> Adapter: onOutcome({status: latency_miss})
Adapter -> SDK: {next: hosted:base-gptq-3b-lowcost}
SDK -> Redwood API: retry -> response

Edge cases / failure modes
- Stale config: adapter should have TTL-based refresh and fallback to a safe default config if refresh fails.
- Conflicting matches: deterministic tie-break rule: lower id lexical order after priority tie.
- Infinite fallback loops: adapter returns terminal after N attempts (configurable, default 3).
- Local policy divergence vs server-side routing: mark mismatch telemetry and surface to ops.

Performance considerations
- Keep evaluation O(number_of_routes_matched), encourage route cardinality < 40 per adapter.
- Avoid heavy predicates: condition DSL should be compiled to bytecode/AST at init.
- Memory: adapter state minimal — policy cache and tokenization hints.
- Network: config refresh must be conditional (If-None-Match) and throttle refreshes (backoff).

Compatibility & migration plan
- v1 config_version: provide strict validator and a compatibility shim in SDK to transform older shapes.
- Beta: ship in SDK behind flag, default server-side behavior unchanged.
- Gradual rollout: provide telemetry-driven gates: measure fallback rates and route mismatch.

Open questions / TODOs
- Condition DSL: decide between JS expressions (flexible but risky) vs small expression language (safer).
- Who owns dynamic pricing signals? local adapter heuristics vs central control plane?
- Should adapter support model quant selection hints (float16/INT8) or leave to runtime? Probably a hint only.
- Privacy: ensure payloadPreview never leaves device. Add enforcement in SDK.
- Do we expose an online editor in Console for simple route preview? Nice UX but scope creep.

Next actionable steps (short-term)
- [ ] Draft a tiny grammar for condition DSL and wire a validator (Priya)
- [ ] Implement route eval microbenchmark (Liam)
- [ ] Create telemetry event schema (Maya)
- [ ] Prototype JS SDK hook with fallback loop (proof-of-concept)

Appendix: compact example (JS)
const cfg = {
  config_version: 1,
  routes: [
    { id: 'qr', match: "labels.intent=='reply_short'", routing:[{candidate:'hosted:fast-2.7b', priority:10}], fallback_policy:{mode:'sequential', max_attempts:2} }
  ]
}

Runner notes (for POC)
- Use a small embedded evaluator (jsep + safe operators) or write a tiny parser.
- Telemetry test harness: record 1000 synthetic requests across label space to validate cardinality and event coverage.

End of sketch.

Sign-off: Maya — quick personal log: keep this intentionally small; the leverage is in stable telemetry + a tiny deterministic policy engine.
